chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
In Quebec, “co-ownership” covers two very distinct realities: divided co-ownership (the classic condo) and undivided co-ownership. They are similar in appearance but differ profoundly in legal, financial and practical terms.

This guide compares the two to help you make an informed choice - because the difference has real-world consequences.

Informative content. Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

In Quebec, “co-ownership” covers two distinct realities: divided (the classic condo) and undivided. They look similar but differ profoundly - legally, financially, on resale. This guide compares them for an informed choice.

The difference has real consequences: this guide gives you the grid to choose.

chapters.title: Divided co-ownership (the classic condo)
chapters.html:
Understand the most common model.

In divided co-ownership, each unit has its own title deed distinct and its batch number.

  • One union of co-ownership manages the building.
  • One declaration of co-ownership regulates rights and obligations.
  • co-ownership charges and a provident fund finance the maintenance.

You finance your unit with your own mortgage: easier to finance and resell.

In divided co-ownership (the classic condo), each unit has its own distinct title and lot number, with a syndicate, a declaration and a contingency fund. You finance it with your own mortgage: it's easier to finance and resell.

Emilie's advice

In division, read the declaration of co-ownership AND the last minutes of the meeting. They reveal upcoming work, conflicts and the real health of the contingency fund.

chapters.title: Undivided co-ownership
chapters.html:
Understand this particular model.

In undivided co-ownership, several people own together ONE building, without division into separate lots.

Everyone has a share of the whole and enjoys a portion according to a joint ownership agreement. There are no separate titles per unit.

  • Often a lower entry price for a given sector.
  • More complex financing: sometimes a joint mortgage.
  • Strong interdependence between co-owners.

In undivided co-ownership, several people together own ONE building, without separate lots: each person holds a share according to a joint ownership agreement. Entry price sometimes lower, but more complex financing (sometimes a joint mortgage) and strong interdependence between co-owners.

Emilie's advice

In undivided ownership, you are linked to the other co-owners, sometimes by a common mortgage. Make sure you know them well and understand the agreement before committing.

chapters.title: Divided or undivided: choose wisely
chapters.html:
Weigh the benefits and risks.

The two models are similar in appearance, but differ profoundly:

  • Divides : simpler, more liquid, better structured - often the default choice.
  • Undivided : sometimes more affordable, but more complex to finance and resell, very dependent on the agreement and the other co-owners.

In both cases: check documents, finances and rules before buying. The right choice depends on your budget and your tolerance for complexity.

At a comparable price, the division offers more peace of mind and is more easily resold; joint ownership can be interesting but go into it with your eyes open, not just to save money. In both cases, check documents, finances and rules before purchasing.

Emilie's advice

At a comparable price, the division offers more peace of mind and is more easily resold. Joint ownership can be interesting, but go into it with your eyes open, not just to save money.

chapters.title: The contingency fund and charges
chapters.objective: Evaluate the financial health of the co-ownership.
chapters.html:
Evaluate the financial health of the co-ownership.

A co-ownership is also a small collective enterprise. Their financial health concerns you directly:

  • Monthly charges : covers routine maintenance and services.
  • Contingency fund : reserve for major repairs (roof, facade, elevator).
  • Study of the provident fund : evaluates whether the reserve is sufficient.

Underfunded fund announces special contributions futures: this is a signal not to be ignored.

Financial health concerns you directly: monthly charges, contingency fund (reserve for roof, facade, elevator), study of the fund. Abnormally low charges are not a godsend: they often hide insufficient funds, and therefore future special contributions.

Emilie's advice

Abnormally low charges are not a godsend: they often hide an insufficient contingency fund. You will pay sooner or later, in the form of a special contribution.

chapters.title: Checks before buying
chapters.html:
Reduce unpleasant surprises.

Before signing, whatever the model, do your documentary inspection:

  1. Read the declaration (divides) or the agreement (undivided).
  2. Consult the minutes and the budget.
  3. Check the status of the provident fund and the planned work.
  4. Confirm the regulations (animals, rental, renovations).

Have these documents examined by your notary: this is the best defense against costly surprises.

Before signing, do your documentary inspection: read the declaration (divided) or the agreement (undivided), the minutes, the budget, the state of the fund and the regulations (animals, rental, renovations). Have these documents reviewed by your notary - it's the best defense against surprises.

Emilie's advice

Always buy a condo “documents in hand”. A poorly read declaration can hide a ban on renting, imminent work or a pending dispute. The notary is your ally here.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Confirm the type of co-ownership of the unit concerned.
  2. Gather the documents (declaration or agreement).

Within 30 days

  1. Have the declaration (divided) or the agreement (undivided) examined.
  2. Check funding implications.

Then

  1. Choose with full knowledge of the facts, with Emilie and the notary.

Before buying

  1. Confirm the type of co-ownership and gather declaration/agreement, finances and minutes.
  2. Have the documents examined by a notary before lifting my conditions.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Divided co-ownership: classic condo, separate title per unit.
  • Undivided co-ownership: share of a single building, without separate lots.
  • Joint ownership agreement: agreement regulating undivided rights and obligations.
  • Provident fund: collective savings (especially divided).
  • Liquidity: ease of resale, generally better in parts.
  • Divided co-ownership: classic condo, separate title per unit.
  • Undivided co-ownership: share of a single building, without separate lots.
  • Joint ownership agreement: agreement regulating undivided rights and obligations.
  • Contingency fund: collective reserve for major repairs.
  • Special contribution: one-off contribution when the fund is not sufficient.
